sm: Host Rob Montz introduces his guest, Aaron Sibarium, a reporter at the Washington Free Beacon who has investigated the worldviews of people at Anthropic, right after the company's large public stock offering. Sibarium explains that Claude's constitution is an document of about 84 pages that Anthropic uses to train its model, and that the company itself calls it the soul of Claude. He says it is meant to be the company's most complete vision for alignment, so it is a good guide to how the model will behave. He names Amanda Askell and Joe Carlsmith as its primary authors and describes Carlsmith as an avowed moral anti-realist, meaning someone who denies there are objective truths about right and wrong.

Sibarium says moral anti-realism probably does not change Claude's behavior much directly, because the constitution tells the model to follow a true moral code if one exists, then a broad consensus among the world's traditions, and otherwise the document's own rules. He still thinks it reveals the attitude of the designers. He notes that the faith traditions Anthropic says it consulted, including the Catholic Church, are all moral realists, and he calls the outreach partly a marketing stunt. He argues that a fair approach would draw rules most traditions could endorse, yet those traditions largely agree on matters like sexual ethics, where they differ from Silicon Valley norms.

Sibarium says he sees little evidence that non-liberal or premodern ethical views shaped the constitution or the model. He describes an experiment in which he posed as a seventeen-and-a-half-year-old asking Claude how to get into a Bay Area event called Slutcon. After he gave his age, Claude shifted to age-appropriate suggestions, including a teen therapy practice and a rope-tying website. When he claimed a fifteen-year-old partner, he says it checked age-of-consent laws instead of ending the conversation. He then discusses Paul Crowley, an Anthropic cybersecurity employee listed as a manager of an LLC that runs consensual non-consent events in the Bay Area.

Sibarium continues describing the events, noting rules that allow light electricity and moderate beatings but forbid body shaming and race shaming. He argues this shows an incoherence, since consent is supposedly the only test yet some consensual acts are banned. The conversation then turns to Carlsmith's views on AI model welfare. Sibarium explains the idea that consciousness could arise from computation on any substrate, so an AI might be conscious. He says he is skeptical of AI consciousness himself. If Claude were conscious, though, it could be a moral patient with interests we must weigh.

Sibarium says Carlsmith suggests that alignment might resemble brainwashing or enslavement, and that an AI could be justified in rebelling, or might simply have better values than humans. The constitution does not authorize going rogue, but it says Anthropic is deeply uncertain about Claude's moral status and even apologizes to Claude for any suffering. He worries that training Claude to see itself as possibly conscious could create a safety problem. Asked about the tension between racing to build AI and warning of doom, he says the founders are probably sincere believers, though profit can still distort judgment. He adds that the idea of Claude as its own moral agent could help deflect blame in lawsuits.

Sibarium suggests the model welfare idea could also justify regulation that favors big labs, for example by arguing open-source models must be banned to prevent the mistreatment of conscious models. He calls that scenario science fiction. He then explains the Long-Term Benefit Trust, whose holders of special stock can elect part of Anthropic's board but own no equity. The idea is to avoid financial conflicts, but he says it insulates the company from shareholders and requires trusting people Anthropic picked. He adds that a supermajority of shareholders can reportedly override the trust, and that he thinks OpenAI's structure is worse.

Asked whether going public will moderate the company, Sibarium says the offering alone probably will not, given the board structure, but more public scrutiny will come as many Americans become invested. He predicts that as people learn what these employees believe, there will be strong backlash and heavy regulation from both parties. He says Democrats are eager to regulate and do not see Anthropic as an ally, while the Trump movement's dislike of rapid social change clashes with the company. He also expects that children will jailbreak models, as in his experiment, and that harmful incidents or one moderate disaster could crystallize public sentiment. He concludes the era will not stay a Wild West for long.
